subject: 😳 Nervous about Nvidia

96 
Plus: The hunt in red October | Monday, November 09, 2026
   
 
 View in browser 
   
 
   
 Axios Markets By
Emily Peck and Matt Phillips
 · 
Nov 09, 2026
 
 
 ☕️ Monday. What a month so far, eh? This morning, U.S. stock futures are pointing up and oil prices down — with benchmark Brent crude at $97 a barrel — ahead of President Trump's meeting in Qatar with a key mediator in the war.

 📉 Nvidia stock fell around 5% in early trading after the company's board said it would conduct an internal investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

 Today, Emily examines how "key man risk" around Huang has moved from a theoretical issue to a real pressing concern for Nvidia investors. Next, we look backward and forward: first, at new Charles Schwab data that shows that retail investors sought to buy the dip last month, and then what to watch for in the week ahead. OK, let's get this party started! In 1,157 words, a 4.5-minute read. 


 
   
   
 
1 big thing: Nvidia's "key man risk" 
 
 By Emily Peck 
   
 
 Data: Financial Modeling Prep ; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios The fallout from Huang's admitted affair with a suspected Chinese spy could reverberate through the entire AI economy.

 Why it matters: The revelations highlight the "key man risk" at Nvidia — the chipmaker's growth and success disproportionately turn on the leather-jacketed superstar who cofounded the company decades ago. 

 What they're saying: "Nvidia is not an ordinary company, and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS NVIDIA, clearly sets the long-term strategy and direction," analysts at Bernstein wrote yesterday evening.

 With Nvidia's flat organizational structure, it's not apparent who could replace him. The big picture: It's not just Nvidia that stands to be affected. The world's largest semiconductor company is at the heart of the AI economy — interconnected with basically all the major players — and Huang is its leading spokesman and policy advocate.

 Nvidia also serves as the central bank of AI, with more than $530 billion in commitments and guarantees to various suppliers, data center operators and cloud computing firms, per this detailed research from Bethany McLean at Hunterbrook. And the $4.5 trillion market-cap company accounts for roughly 7% of the S&P 500 index. Catch up quick: Yesterday, Huang admitted to having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, and the company's board announced it was launching an independent investigation.

 What to watch: Whether the investigation shakes the board's confidence in the charismatic leader and what its shares do today.

 Where it stands: The company's stock fell sharply last week on worries that the midterm election results were a setback for the data center build-out.

 On Friday, Nvidia stock closed at $186.64 — down 6% from a year ago and on track for its worst annual performance since 2022 , before the ChatGPT-sparked AI gold rush sent its stock into the stratosphere. Its stock is now down 22% from its October peak. Between the lines: The espionage allegations and Huang's admitted affair are obviously a bad look for the CEO and his company.

 At a minimum, they could hurt politically —  giving congressional China hawks ammunition to further curtail trade with the country and provide ammo to a newly elected wave of anti-AI lawmakers. Headlines reading "Nvidia's CEO got honeypotted by China" are "going to be a heavy distraction, and at the worst provide significant ammunition to both sides of the aisle," the Bernstein analysts wrote. Reality check: Nvidia already had an interest in getting the U.S. to let it sell more chips in China —  it didn't really need a spy to convince it. 

 "This seems superfluous to us," the analysts wrote. The intrigue: Whispers about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore data center firm Megaspeed, surfaced back in May. 

 Short-seller Culper Research alleged that Nvidia chips were getting to Chinese customers through Megaspeed, claiming it was financed by Alibaba. Yes, but: Culper's claims are not proven, and it's not clear if any sensitive information was compromised. 

 The other side: Nvidia's board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised and expressed confidence in Huang's leadership, Axios' Madison Mills reported . 

 Go deeper: The crisis testing Nvidia's "too big to fail" CEO 


 
 
   
   
 
2. Schwab: Investors looked for a bounce back
 
 By Jeffrey Cane 
   
 
 
 
 Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images


 
   
 
 Retail investors were more willing to place bets on individual stocks last month after preferring exchange-traded funds (ETFs) in September, new data from Charles Schwab shared exclusively with Axios indicates.

 "I think they were waiting for a pullback in October and they got it," says Joe Mazzola, head trading strategist at Schwab, referring to retail investors who took advantage of a dip in prices to pour into semiconductor and AI-adjacent companies. Why it matters: Such optimism among ordinary individual investors is now being put to the test after a rocky start this month.

 Zoom out: October was peak earnings season, and for some tech stocks that had disappointing results or outlooks, like Intel , investors saw the resulting selloffs as perhaps overdone and an opportunity to buy, Mazzola says.

 In addition to Intel, some of the most popular stocks bought by Schwab clients in October included SpaceX, Nvidia, Micron Technology and Alphabet. By the numbers: The Schwab Trading Activity Index, or STAX, climbed to 61.94 in October, from 58.92 in September, per a release out this morning.

 Schwab says that its index shows what investors were actually doing in the market each month, as it is calculated by analyzing the stock positions and trading activity of its millions of client accounts. Reality check: While net buying overall was up for the month, only three of the S&P 500 index's 11 sectors — communication services, information technology and industrials — were beneficiaries, as investors sought out growth stocks.

3. 👀 Inflation data could pile more pressure on stocks
 
 By Matt Phillips 
   
 
 Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios After a wobbly post-election performance last week, investor focus will be back on inflation this week and its implications for the Federal Reserve. 

 Why it matters: New price data could convince diehard believers in the " Fed put ," that the central bank will not, in fact, swoop to steady a stock market battered by the Blue Tsunami's implications for AI.

 What we're watching: Consumer Price Index data tomorrow — and producer prices on Friday.

 By the numbers: Wall Street analysts expect headline inflation to be up 3.9% over October 2025 levels. (Ex-food and energy would be up 2.7%.)

 The headline PPI index due Friday is expected to be up 6.7% in October, compared with the prior year, showing price pressures continue to build. Between the lines: The risks to stocks are pretty one-sided. 

 If inflation numbers are higher than expected, that could mean a steeper, faster series of rate hikes that could add pressure to stocks. But if inflation undershoots expectations, few think that will keep the central bank from lifting rates, as recent jobs data has shown the economy to be quite strong.
